sections.title: 6. How to Approach MCM Style Problems

blocks.text: Matrix Chain Multiplication, or MCM, is the poster child of interval DP. It answers a subtle question: given a chain of matrices to multiply, in what order should we multiply them to do the least work?
The product is the same no matter how we group the multiplications, but the cost can differ enormously. MCM finds the cheapest grouping.

blocks.caption: Every way of placing parentheses gives the same product but a very different cost

blocks.text: Multiplying an a by b matrix with a b by c matrix costs a times b times c scalar multiplications and produces an a by c matrix.
Matrix multiplication is associative, so (A B) C equals A (B C). But the number of operations to get there is not the same. One grouping can be many times cheaper than another.

items: A chain like A x B x C x D has many valid parenthesizations
All of them yield the identical final matrix
Each ordering has its own multiplication cost
We want the ordering with the minimum total cost

blocks.text:
Concrete intuition:

With matrices sized 10x100, 100x5, and 5x50, one grouping costs 7500 operations and the other costs 75000. Same answer, ten times the work.
We represent the chain of n matrices with a single dimension array p of length n plus one. Matrix i has dimensions p[i minus 1] by p[i].
This compact trick works because the columns of one matrix must equal the rows of the next, so consecutive dimensions are shared. One array captures the whole chain.
Define dp[i][j] as the minimum cost to multiply the matrices from i to j into a single matrix. We try every place to make the last multiplication, at split point k.

blocks.caption: Split the chain at k, solve both sides, then pay to multiply the two resulting matrices

blocks.text: Splitting at k means we first form the product of i to k and of k plus one to j, then multiply those two results together. That final step costs p[i minus 1] times p[k] times p[j].

codes.python:
# dp[i][j] = min cost to multiply matrices i..j
for k in range(i, j):
    cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j]
    dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], cost)

blocks.text: Just like interval DP, we loop by chain length so smaller chains are ready before larger ones. A single matrix costs nothing, so those cells stay at zero.
The complexity is O(n cubed) in time and O(n squared) in space, the standard interval DP cost.
MCM is worth mastering because its exact structure reappears in many problems.

items: Burst Balloons: identical split-at-k reasoning with a different merge cost.
Minimum Cost Tree from Leaf Values: build a tree by combining adjacent ranges.
Boolean Parenthesization: count ways to parenthesize a boolean expression.
Optimal Binary Search Tree: choose a root for each range to minimise search cost.

blocks.text: If you can solve MCM cleanly, you can adapt it to all of these by changing only the merge cost.

content.title: 6. How to Approach MCM Style Problems

blocks.text: Reach for this pattern when you must decide an order of combining a linear sequence.

items: Notice you are combining adjacent items and the order affects the cost.
Encode the chain compactly, often with a dimensions array.
Define dp[i][j] as the best cost to fully combine the range i to j.
Try every split k and add the cost of merging the two resulting pieces.
Iterate by chain length so sub-chains are solved first, then read dp over the full range.

blocks.text: MCM is the cleanest way to internalise interval DP. Once it clicks, the whole family opens up.
